The 10215th meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is: the situation in the Middle East. The agenda is adopted. In accordance with rule 37 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the representatives of Qatar, the Syrian Arab Republic and Turkey to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. In accordance with Rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the following briefers to participate in this meeting: Mr. Claudio Cordone, Deputy Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria, Mr. Indrika Rajadatte, Acting Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Deputy Emergency Relief Coordinator, and Ms. Rula Rugby, Country Director of Women Now for Development, Lebanon. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item two of the agenda. I now give the floor to Mr. Claudio Cordone.

Thank you, Madam President. And I'm briefing you from Damascus following the Secretary-General's visit to Syria last month, the first by a Secretary-General in 17 years. Let me at the outset thank the Syrian authorities for all the efforts made to ensure a secure and open environment for all his engagements. In his meetings with President al-Sharaa, Foreign Minister Shihbani, and other senior officials, the Secretary-General welcomed progress in Syria's political transition, including steps to strengthen state institutions and towards reconciliation, accountability, and transitional justice. He stressed that the success of the political transition will ultimately be measured by whether all Syrians feel represented in state institutions, and able to participate meaningfully in shaping their country's future. He shared this message during his open engagements with a wide array of Syrian women, civil society, and diverse communities. The Secretary-General was equally clear that Syria cannot meet the transition challenges alone. Greater international support is essential to meet urgent humanitarian recovery, and development needs and create conditions for safe, dignified and voluntary returns. Syrians need tangible improvements in their daily lives and the viable future in their country. International support is essential to the success of the political transition itself. Madam President, I welcome the US rescinding of Syria's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism. These steps should help create more favorable conditions for economic recovery, investment, and broader international engagement with Syria. According to an International Monetary Fund mission that visited Damascus last month, recovery is accelerating and double-digit growth in 2026 is projected. But widespread poverty and renewed inflation mean conditions remain very difficult for most Syrians. Madam President, the People's Assembly has adopted rules of procedures and we await the beginning of its substantive work, including on a host of legislative priorities. Further clarity is needed on the Assembly's oversight role regarding the executive. Its independence and transparency will be important to the Assembly's credibility and to fostering public trust and international confidence in the transition. The process for drafting a permanent constitution is also yet to be specified. We encourage an inclusive, transparent and participatory process capable of forging a new social contract for Syria. There is urgency in starting this process, as in preparing for the elections at the end of the transition. and my office stands ready to provide technical support and advice. Madam President, this month, the Damascus Fourth Criminal Court convicted and sentenced to death several former officials, including former President Bashar al-Assad, who along with others was tried in absentia, as well as Hatif Najib and Waseem al-Assad, who appeared in person. Ahmed Hassoun, former Grand Mufti, was also tried in person and received a life sentence. The proceedings incorporated several important fair trial safeguards for the defendants present in court, and there is a right of appeal within 30 days. However, fair trial safeguards should be strengthened by reinforcing effective legal representation, and ensuring a full appeal on the facts, not just on points of law. Greater consistency with fair trial standards will strengthen confidence in the fairness of integrity of the transitional justice process and ensure that guilt is assigned to individual perpetrators and not to groups. And consistent with UN policy and as called for by the General Assembly, I urge the Syrian authorities to establish a moratorium on all executions. On 21 August, I attended the commemoration of the chemical attack in Eastern Ghouta and Madamiyah, which killed some 1,500 and left thousands injured. I expressed my solidarity with the victims and survivors, my regret that the international community failed to prevent these atrocities, and underscored the need for full accountability for those responsible. Madam President, Israeli military activity has continued in southern Syria, including repeated ground incursions, house searches, and the destruction of private and agricultural property, particularly in Quneitra and the Yarmouk Basin. I note the release of a number of Syrians held in Israeli detention, but remain concerned by continuing detentions, and families are seeking information on the fate and whereabouts of their detained relatives. I'm also concerned by statements from senior Israeli officials advocating an open-ended military Israeli military presence on Syrian territory. The continued Israeli presence east of the ceasefire line violates Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity and is inconsistent with the 1974 disengagement of forces agreement. Let me also reiterate as the Secretary General did during his visit, that the Golan Heights remain occupied Syrian territory in accordance with international law and relevant Security Council and General Assembly resolutions. Another worrying development was the Israeli airstrike on the Abu Dhur airbase in northern Syria on 18th August, which I condemn. I welcome the recent direct Israel-Syria contacts and talks in Jordan, and support the United States efforts to mediate a security arrangement between Syria and Israel and the operation of the confliction mechanism. Diplomacy must prevail and negotiation should progress within the framework of international law. Madam President, Syria continues to face significant internal security challenges. Although overall violence declined in August from July, violent criminal acts, continue to be frequently reported, particularly killings perceived by local communities as retaliatory attacks against specific groups. Civil society organizations continue to report disappearances of women, men, and children. While some individuals have returned to their families, including an eight-year-old girl this month, others have been found dead, and many remain unaccounted for. Deaths in custody, possibly resulting from torture have been reported. A commission of inquiry established by the Ministry of Interior found that Mohammed of Meira died as a result of physical abuse inflicted during interrogation in custody. I condemn this and send my condolences to his family. I welcome the Minister's commitment to hold accountable responsible personnel while urging a clear and sustained public government position against any abuses in detention, as well as enhanced guidelines and training. Effective law enforcement will be essential to efforts to rebuild a society in which all citizens feel protected from violence and abuses. The Ministry of Interior's efforts to train women police officers represent a positive step, particularly in strengthening responses to crimes affecting women and girls. I also wish to stress that the threat posed by terrorism, specifically Daesh, remains a serious concern. Earlier this month, the Syrian authorities announced the arrest of a prominent Daesh commander as part of continuing efforts to pursue Daesh leaders and networks. And sustained counter-terrorism efforts consistent with international law remain essential. Madam President, I welcome the important progress achieved in the 25 August meeting between President al-Sharaa and Maslum Abdi, marking continuing steps forward on security and administrative integration of northeastern Syria. And I particularly welcome the announcement of Maslum Abdi at the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and their dissolution. I know the importance of the issue of education and look forward to further progress on that issue. I also note that further discussions have taken place between the Minister of Interior and the women's protection units on that latter's integration. And I reiterate our support for the full implementation of the 29th January agreement and the readiness of the United Nations to provide support on the ground. I note at the same time that the first convoy of returnees to Ras al-Ayn was attacked on 10th August, triggering tensions that spread to Ain al-Arab, Kobani, Hasakah and elsewhere, underscoring the potential for localized tensions to challenge broader progress. Madam President, Syria continues to be characterized by a political and security stalemate. Relations between local actors and the authorities in Damascus remain marked by mutual distrust, with some actors continuing to call for independence or joining Israel. Long-standing grievances remain unresolved, particularly those concerning accountability, although trials of some of the alleged perpetrators started in July. A concerning incident involving the desecration of Christian graves was reported in Al-Sawara Al-Kubra, an area under government control in northern countryside of Sweida. following earlier similar reports involving Drew's grades. We take note of the presidential decree of 17 August providing for an exceptional examination session for students who missed their examination last June. There are concerns about the location of the examination centers and about how many students would actually sit the examination. And there are reports indicating attempts from within Sweida to prevent students from traveling to sit for their examination. We remain ready to support the implementation of the September 2025 roadmap, including the returns of displaced Druze and Bedouin populations and addressing the issues of detainees and the missing, while remaining guided by Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Madam President, ensuring the meaningful participation of all segments of society remains essential. In Damascus, Syrian women shared with the Secretary-General their views on a broad set of issues, including the recognition of all victims as part of a transitional justice strategy, the importance of proper investigation of allegations of abductions and sexual assaults, of Syrian women and the importance of greater representation of women in decision-making positions, as well as their meaningful participation in the recovery and reconstruction efforts. And I'm pleased that the Council will have the opportunity to hear more of these issues from Rula Rukabeh. Syrian women remain an extraordinary reservoir of experience and capacity. Their efforts to build a Syrian state that meets the expectation of Syrian women and indeed all Syrians predate this transition. For more than a decade, the Office of the Special Envoy has benefited from the Women's Advisory Board's invaluable contribution to mediation efforts. With the change of circumstances on the ground, we conducted an extensive consultation process to explore how best to continue this strong engagement with Syrian women. We will now expand our outreach to Syrian women, discuss themes of their choosing, and share their recommendations with the government. Although the board held its final meeting in July, its members will continue contributing to the transition. And I thank them for their commitment and advice, and the donors for their support over the years. Civil society organizations likewise emphasize inclusion and participation in their meeting with the Secretary General, welcoming progress while calling for judicial and security sector reform, accountability, an inclusive transitional justice project, process, equal rights, and the protection of civic space. And the discussions showcase the range and depth of civil society and the contributions they can make to Syria's successful transition. Madam President, before concluding, allow me to underline the continuing cooperation with the Syrian authorities. Together, we are collaborating on areas of mutual interest and doing so in close coordination with the UN country team. Our objective remains to develop further such cooperation through the presence of a restructured office in Damascus. And we will continue to build on this progress with the support of the Council, guided by our shared commitment to Syria's successful transition. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank Mr. Cordone for his briefing. And I now give the floor to Mr. Enrique Ratuati.

Madam President, I thank Deputy Special Envoy Ghosn for his continued efforts to advocate for the and support for the people of Syria. Last week, I was in Syria and had the opportunity to travel to Deir Ezzor, Al Raqqa, Aleppo and Idlib and met with communities, humanitarian partners and the authorities. My central message is simple. Syria is at a pivotal moment and Syrians are hopeful for a stable and prosperous future. After years of conflict, displacement and economic decline, there are encouraging signs of revival. More Syrians are returning home. Agricultural production is improving, with reports suggesting that this year's wheat harvest could allow Syria to achieve seasonal self-sufficiency. Energy and transport networks are gradually recovering. Commercial activity is increasing. and humanitarian access remains broadly improved compared with previous years. These developments matter because they offer something Syrians have lacked for too long, hope that recovery is possible. The government remains steadfast in consolidating fragile stability into sustainable development and economic growth. The international community must seize this opportunity and support the aspirations of the Syrian people. But optimism must be tempered with realism. Humanitarian needs still remain immense. Millions of people still struggle to access healthcare, food, clean water, education and livelihoods. And the gap between needs and available resources is growing. Syria is experiencing the largest voluntary return movement in the region in over a decade. Nearly 2 million internally displaced people and more than 1.7 million refugees have returned to their communities since December 2024. But return does not mean the end of humanitarian need. For many families, it is the beginning of another struggle in rebuilding their lives. Homes remain damaged or destroyed. Basic services are struggling to absorb rapidly growing populations. Schools, hospitals, water systems need rehabilitation. Access to livelihoods remain extremely limited. However, dealing with unexploded ordinance and mines as well as rubble removal continue to be a key enabler. At the same time, more than 5.5 million people remain internally displaced, including some 830,000 people living in more than 1,200 camps. The challenge is therefore to ensure that returns are safe, voluntary and dignified, to enable sustainable reintegration in their areas of origin, and that people have what they need to stay. In this context, the Government's No Tents, No Camps initiative reflects an important objective, moving families from prolonged displacement towards durable and sustainable solutions. Humanitarians stand ready to support these efforts, working in close collaboration with recovery and development actors, in coordination with the government. Madam President, as families return home and as communities begin to recover, another danger comes into sharper focus, explosive ordinance. Since December 2024, the grim reality is that close to 1,400 explosive ordinance incidents have caused more than 2,400 casualties, including 865 deaths and nearly 1,600 injuries. Sadly, 22 of those deaths and 47 of those injuries have taken place just since the 17th of July. Many, most incidents took place in agricultural and grazing areas. Farmers working their lands, shepherds moving livestock, children playing outdoors. These are everyday acts that carry deadly risks. Mine action in Syria is not optional. It's essential for safe returns, agricultural recovery and economic revival. Progress is possible in 2024. Mine Action partners surveyed 215 million square meters of land. And in 2025, that increased 18-fold to 4 billion square meters, roughly five times the size of New York City. While these, while that nearly three times as much as explosive ordinance has been identified and destroyed, but the scale of contamination remains immense. Expanded survey and clearance operations, risk education and mine action support must keep pace and be scaled up. Madam President, the humanitarian community continues to deliver across Syria. In the first six months of this year, we and our humanitarian partners reached an average of 2.4 million people each month with food, clean water, lifesaving medical procedures and protection services. The Syria Humanitarian Fund has just launched a 70 million allocation to support safe and dignified returns, community integration, explosive hazard clearance and rapid humanitarian response across the country. At the same time, a separate 5 million allocation will support partners delivering assistance to communities in dire need in southern Syria. Syrian organizations are at the heart of all humanitarian efforts. representing nearly 60% of the partners on the ground. But we have been asked to do more with less. This is not a realistic ask. Even after we prioritise the most severe needs and reduce funding requirements by one third, the Syria Humanitarian Appeal is only 30% funded at this point. This is precisely the moment when investment can turn fragile progress into lasting recovery. Such progress will reverberate in Syria with significant positive implications for the region and beyond. Syria needs investments to realize its vision of transitioning out of humanitarian need into reconstruction and development. Funding the humanitarian response to mitigate acute vulnerabilities and systemic fragility fosters stability and enables recovery. These are investments in key sectors that lay the foundation for scalable, sustainable investments in rebuilding a nation. Syria is demonstrating that change and transformation is not just possible, it is attainable. Madam President, in conclusion, I have three asks. First, commit to sustained and flexible funding for humanitarian and development action. Invest in the future that the Syrian people aspire to. Secondly, invest in durable solutions for displaced people and returnees, alongside robust reconstruction and economic recovery efforts led by the Syrian government. Thirdly, prevent Syria from being drawn into regional conflict, which should bring more displacement, division, deprivation and instability to people who have already endured far too much. Progress remains fragile, but it is real. Often in this Council, we have debated and discussed complex and intractable situations with no resolution in sight. The message I heard across Syria was clear. People want the opportunity to rebuild their lives. They would like to see the international community support to fulfill this aspiration. This is not a moment to step back. It is a moment to invest in the stability, in stability and progress. This is the moment to show our solidarity with the people of Syria and turn hope into recovery and prosperity. Madam President, it's a carpe diem moment and the moment is now and we should seize it. I thank you.
And I thank Mr. Wathwate for his briefing. And I now give the floor to Ms. Rula Roubi, to Fethiye.

Madam President, Excellencies, thank you for providing this space for a voice from Syrian feminist civil society. My name is Rula Rukbi, a daughter of the city of Hama, and I carry with me the memory of one of the largest mass atrocities committed by the former regime against Syrians. Government forces killed approximately 30,000 civilians in February 1982. I am here today as the country director of Women Now for Development Lebanon. For 14 years, our work has been guided by one central principle: change must begin from the bottom and reach the top. After years of war, repression, displacement, and loss, many Syrians welcomed the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 with joy and hope. hope that it would bring an end not only to war but also to authoritarianism, fear and exclusion. Since power has changed hands in Syria, the most important question has been: what kind of state are we building after this change? Are we building a state in which every Syrian feels that they are equal citizens? Or are we recreating a similar system under a new name? We have serious concerns about excessive centralization, the absence of an effective separation of powers, and the lack of clarity around governance, transparency, and accountability, alongside the deteriorating economic situation. Syrians still do not clearly know how decisions are made, by whom, or how those decision-makers can be held accountable. And this is where one of the greatest risks of the transition lies. that we change the people in power without changing the way power is exercised. A genuine transition means building a new relationship between the state and its citizens, one in which the rule of law applies to everyone and protects everyone equally. Madam President, Syrian women have paid an enormous price throughout the conflict. They have endured displacement, poverty, violence, detention and disappearance, and continue to bear the brunt of the ongoing humanitarian crisis alongside entrenched legal and social discrimination. Despite this, Syrian women have played a leading role in documenting human rights violations, providing aid to their communities, and advocating for justice and accountability, including for missing persons. While at the international level we see positive efforts by the Syrian transitional authorities to recognize the important role of women, for instance, in the context of the search for missing persons, women still find themselves at the margins when it comes to decisions about the country's future at home. For instance, women's representation in parliament is less than 11% and only one member of the transitional cabinet is a woman. But this is not a matter of numbers. Meaningful participation means women being present when decisions are made, not only when photos are being taken. Women's rights and personal and civil liberties are not issues that can be deferred, including the reform of nationality and personal status laws, stronger protections against gender-based violence, and removing serious reservations to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. A state that does not recognize women as full and equal citizens cannot be democratic, regardless of what its political system is called. Reports of the abduction of women and girls since December 2024, particularly from the Alawite community, are deeply alarming. Targeting women because of their sectarian identity or using violence against them to take revenge or instill fear in their communities perpetuates precisely the patterns of violence that Syria must overcome. This brings me to transitional justice. Syria needs justice that does not select its victims. For decades, Syrians were subjected to violations, including arbitrary detention, torture, and enforced disappearance at the hands of the former regime. Civilians also suffered abuses at the hands of non-state armed groups and other actors. But violations did not end with the fall of the regime. Today, people continue to be arbitrarily detained for expressing opinions. We also hear troubling reports of torture and ill-treatment in detention facilities, including most recently the death of a former White Helmet, Mohammed Gamirah, following alleged torture while in detention. Violence on the Syrian coast and in Suwayda involving security forces and local armed groups has also led to serious violations, including killings of civilians and sexual and gender-based violence, some of which has taken on sectarian and retaliatory dimensions targeting Alawite and Druze communities alongside a rise in hate speech targeting different Syrian communities. Victims of the former regime and different armed groups and victims of violations committed since December 2024 have the same right to truth and justice. A victim is a victim and the violation is a violation regardless of who committed it. If the new Syria is built on Making a distinction between victims who deserve justice and those who can be ignored, we will be planting the seeds of the next conflict. Genuine reconciliation must be built on truth, recognition, accountability, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence. Excellencies, rebuilding Syria is not only about rebuilding roads and homes. It is about rebuilding trust, trust between citizens and the state, trust amongst Syrians themselves. and trust that the law exists to protect people, not to be used as a weapon against them. Return to Syria must also be voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable. It must be linked to social protection and reconstruction that serves people. including by providing support for those who have lost their homes and developing cooperative and social housing so that return does not simply mean moving from displacement into poverty and insecurity. The UN also bears a fundamental responsibility. We recognize the necessity of engaging constructively with the Syrian transitional authorities and working with them. However, international support for the political transition must be linked to clear benchmarks on human rights, the rule of law, and accountability. The desire for stability in Syria should not lead to the acceptance of shrinking civic space, restrictions on freedoms, or selective justice and accountability. We have learned at an enormous human cost that stability built on fear and silence is not peace. It merely defers the next crisis. Madam President, I conclude with four recommendations for the Security Council and the UN. First, human rights, including women's rights, must be at the center of the UN's evolving role in Syria. Human rights, civic space, women's full, equal, meaningful and safe participation, accountability and the rule of law must remain integral to the UN's political engagement with the Syrian transitional authorities and must be central to any new UN presence in Syria. Second, maintain strong and independent human rights scrutiny. Security Council members should continue to support independent UN human rights and accountability mechanisms and should encourage the Syrian transitional authorities to ensure full cooperation and effective access to these mechanisms. The UN should also continue to follow accountability processes concerning violations on the Syrian coast and in Sweida. while emphasizing transparency, compliance with international standards, and responsibility at all levels, including command responsibility. Third, help protect and expand Syria's civic space. The space that Syrians have today to organize, speak, and engage publicly remains fragile. The UN should continue to monitor restrictions on freedom of expression, freedom of association and freedom of peaceful assembly, and regulations on political parties, as well as arbitrary detention and reprisals against journalists, human rights defenders and civil society actors, including women. Fourth, press for rights-based institutional and security sector reform. This should include effective checks and balances on executive power, judicial independence, and independent civilian and institutional oversight of security institutions, transparent vetting, and clear chains of command. International engagement and support should also help ensure that new institutions do not reproduce old patterns of unchecked power. They should also help ensure that new institutions do not allow individuals credibly implicated in serious violations to exercise authority without scrutiny or accountability. At the same time, we urge the Syrian transitional authorities to engage fully with the independent civil society and relevant UN mechanisms to translate these principles into action. Excellencies, The question that must remain at the heart of every discussion about Syria is the following: How do we prevent the return of the conditions that led to war? The answer begins with a state that protects human dignity and freedom, a state in which women are full and equal citizens, not guests at the decision-making table. A sovereign state in which young Syrians can find a future instead of fear. a future instead of fear, weapons or migration, and a system of justice that respects every victim, regardless of who they are or who committed the violation against them. And I firmly believe that it is not too late. We still have an opportunity to build Syria in which people do not fear the state but trust it to protect them. A Syria that has room for all its children and does not allow what they have endured to be repeated. This is the transition that all Syrians deserve. And this is the peace that can last. Thank you.
I thank Ms. Ruckeburn for her briefing, and I now give the floor to those Council members who wish to make statements. I give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, Madam President, and thank you to today's briefers, of course. Colleagues, the United States rescinded its designation of Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism on August 24th, a historic milestone that recognizes the progress the Syrian authorities continue to make on political, humanitarian, and security priorities. Lifting U.S. restrictions on Syria will continue to unlock international trade and investment opportunities, contributing to the rebuilding of Syria. A stable, unified Syria at peace with itself and its neighbors will also enhance peace and security for those in the region and beyond. We look forward to further supporting Syria's counterterrorism efforts By building on its membership in the global coalition to defeat ISIS, the United States also applauds Iraq and Syria's July 17th announcement to advance rehabilitation of the Iraq-Syria crude oil pipeline, restoring a critical energy corridor which will make energy more accessible to the global market. We welcome the engagement of a US-led consortium on this project, which advances security and stability through prosperity for both countries. This progress reflects the vision and leadership of President Trump to build a more prosperous and interconnected region. We reiterate our call for UN institutions and member states to support the Syrian government's efforts to advance these goals. We urge the International Impartial and Independent Mechanism, the Triple I.M., and the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in Syria, the IIMP, to work with the Syrian government to finalize MOUs that will enable both of those parties and Syria to provide resources to support the ongoing transitional justice project in Syria. We take note of the IAEA's productive recent visit to Syria and welcome cooperation between the Syrian government and the IAEA toward fulfilling Syria's safeguard obligations related to the Treaty of the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons in a safe and expeditious manner. We also call on both Israel and Syria to seek de-escalation in the aftermath of the August 18th airstrikes on the Abu al-Duhur airbase. The United States will continue to engage closely with both countries and with all regional stakeholders to promote dialogue and peaceful solutions. As we look ahead to high level week next month, we encourage members of this council and all member states to use this opportunity for meaningful engagement with the Syrian government in support of a stable, secure, and prosperous Syria. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

Madam President, We thank the Deputy Special Envoy, Secretary-General Claudio Cordone, and Acting Assistant Secretary-General Indrika Ratwatte for their briefings and assessment of the situation in Syria. We have heard from the civil society representative, Rola Rugbi. We welcome to this meeting Syria, Qatar, and Turkey. Russia is interested in the earliest possible normalization of the situation in the friendly country of Syria. strengthening its sovereignty and state institutions. We support the focus of Damascus on upholding, protecting the rights of all Syrian citizens, regardless of their ethnic or religious backgrounds. We believe that it is this approach that is the key to an inclusive political process in line with the key provisions of the cornerstone resolution of Security Council 2054. We know with satisfaction the progress achieved by the Syrian authorities in this regard. In particular, they've successfully reintegrated the northeastern regions of the country and they have completed the process of forming the new People's Assembly. We hope that these steps will help to strengthen the unity of the Syrian Arab Republic, and the launch of the parliament's work will give the requisite impetus to the process of adopting a new constitution and other legislation. At the same time, we note that any decisions adopted by all branches of Syrian authority ought to be strictly and unfailingly based upon clearly laid out legal norms and meet the standards of a state governed by rule of law. the same time, we must note a number of serious challenges and obstacles to the efforts of the Syrian people and government to guarantee lasting stabilization. First of all, it concerns the continuing aggressive actions by Israel on Syrian territory. The latest flagrant examples of this have been the strikes by the Israeli Air Force on the Abu Zukour air base in the province of Idlib on August 18th, as well as drone attacks on a vehicle near the town of Beit Jine, which led to civilian casualties. These military actions by the IDF, together with the continued occupation of Syrian territory, are a clear violation of international law and the sovereignty of the Syrian Arab Republic and they undermine efforts to fully resolve the situation in the country. We call on West Jerusalem to stop these military escapades. We remind the Israeli government of the need to fully and unconditionally implement the Disengagement of Forces Agreement of 1974. Continued terrorist activity still poses serious risks for Syria and its people. Bus bombings in the suburbs of Damascus on August 6 and 22 have been an alarming reminder of this. They led to the injuries of several civilians and law enforcement officers. We note that the Syrian authorities continue, we hope they will continue to take concrete measures to combat terrorist threats, including through including foreign combatants, and will bring the perpetrators to justice. We hope that we'd like to call on the international community to consolidate efforts to combat terrorist attacks in the Middle East and beyond its borders. Madam President, the situation on the humanitarian front remains alarming. Seventy percent of Syria's population still needs aid. At the same time, the OCHA country humanitarian plan, which is already highly prioritized, has been funded only at the level of 30 percent. Under these circumstances, we have a positive view of the new allocations from the UN Humanitarian Fund for Syria in the amount of $75 million, which will go to supporting the return of Syrians and their reintegration, as well as the clearing of Syrian territory from explosive objects. It's important for this international assistance to go not only toward current needs but also toward rebuilding infrastructure and restoring income sources. It is this transition from emergency aid to normalizing the economic and social life of the country that Syria needs. We welcome the close work of the UN bodies with national agencies. Humanitarian aid ought to complement and bolster local capacities instead of replacing them. And here we believe that this is the key element to a true localization of humanitarian activity. We see signs of broader economic revival in Syria. The IMF this year expects double-digit economic growth rates thanks to a recovery of agriculture and an expansion in hydrocarbon extraction as well as electricity generation. and the revival of trade and services. Of course, these positive trends do not mean that accumulated problems caused by or exacerbated by inflation pressure and weak banking systems have been fully resolved. In this regard, we note the decision of the World Bank to provide Syria with a grant in the amount of $100 million to strengthen the financial sector of the country. The facilitation of banking operations, stimulation of trade and investment, will be aided by the August 24 removal of Syria from the US list of states sponsors of terrorism. We reaffirm our principled position, which we uphold beyond Syria as well, that is the need to fully refrain from the use of unilateral coercive measures. We cannot, at the same time, call on Syrians to return home and speak of the need to maintain the country's independence while setting up barriers to the country's normal economic functioning. Only a combination of humanitarian aid and full restoration of the national economy can provide Syria with a lasting way out of this longstanding crisis. President, we hope that the Security Council and the international community will take concrete measures to support the authorities in Syria. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Madam President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the A3, namely the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and my own country, Somalia. We thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone and Acting ASG Ratwatte for their comprehensive and insightful updates. We have listened carefully to the remarks of Mr. Rogbe and we welcome the participation of the permanent representative of Syria in today's meeting. Madam President, the A3 recognizes that Syria is making meaningful strides in its political, security, and economic development, even at it confronts significant challenges. Encouraging recent progress has opened new possibilities for national stability, but their credibility will depend on inclusive participation, effective representation of women and all communities, accountability, and institutions that function independently and transparently. Emphasizing that overcoming ongoing difficulties will require continued united support from the international community to help Syrians build a brighter and more prosperous future. The high-level diplomatic engagement of the United Nations with Syria's transitional authorities, highlighted by the Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' historic visit to Damascus and his engagement with the Syrian leadership, civil society and minority communities is testimony to this progress. We reiterate our strong support for the vital work of the Special Envoy's Office and reaffirmed that Security Council Resolution 2254 remains the essential framework for sustainable Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political settlement. Turning to the humanitarian situation, we remain gravely concerned. Millions of Syrians continue to depend on life-saving assistance, while the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan is severely underfunded with only about one third of the required resources secured. Although over two million internally displaced persons and nearly 1.8 million refugees have reportedly returned, millions more remain displaced inside Syria or as refugees abroad. Sustainable returns demand safety, adequate housing, schools and health facilities, livelihoods, documentation, protection services and essential public utilities. Humanitarian relief, early recovery and reconstruction must therefore advance in tandem. We are encouraged by the improved humanitarian access across most of the Syria with an average of 2.4 million people reached monthly in the first half of 2026. Though we note that localized access challenges and services gap persist, including in the south and part of the northeast. Therefore, we urgently call on international donors to increase predictable and flexible support, financial support to bridge critical shortfalls and ensure the continuity of essential services. Explosive ordinance remain a major impedent to save returns, livelihoods and recovery. Since the council's last meeting, there have been reported 53 explosive ordinance incidents resulting in 20 fatalities, especially in agriculture and grazing areas. The A3 calls for an increased international support for mine action, clearance activities, risk education and victim assistance measures that are indispensable for civilian protection, food security and sustainable returns. We also recognize the vital connection between economic recovery and lasting stability. The A3 welcomes recent steps that facilitate Syria's reintegration into the global economy and trade system. including the removal of restrictive designations, the lifting of sanctions barriers, and Syria's removal from the state sponsors of terrorism lists. This paves the way for correspondent banking and foreign investment. As ordinary citizens continue to face inflation and liquidity constraints, we stress that economic stabilization and investment in public utilities and basic infrastructure are vital for long-term recovery. At the same time, we remain deeply alarmed by the persistent violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity. We deplore the recent military strikes and incursions inside Syrian territory, including the August 18th and 19th airstrikes in eastern Idlib. Syria must not become a theater for broader confrontation. Furthermore, the heightened security posture along the Golan Heights and Mount Hermon buffer zone threaten to undermine Syria's recovery efforts as well as risk regional stability. The A3 reiterates that the occupied Syrian Golan is an integral part of Syria in line with Security Council Resolution 497 of 1981 and calls for full respect for Syria's sovereignty a strict adherence to the 1974 disengagement agreement, and support for efforts to prevent border friction. Terrorism and internal insecurity continue to pose grave threats to Syria and the wider region. The AT unequivocally condemns the terrorist attack that targeted Syria's internal security forces on August 23rd. As the transitional authorities undertake stabilization operations, to neutralize violent extremism networks, including ISIL-Daesh in central and unstable areas across the country. We emphasize that robust international cooperation, coordination, and capacity building are essential to preventing any resurgence of terrorism in Syria and beyond. In closing, Madam President, the A3 reaffirms its unwavering commitment to Syria's sovereignty, unity, independence, and territorial integrity. We urge the Security Council and the international community to remain steadfast in supporting Syria's journey toward lasting peace, reconciliation, and prosperity, so that all Syrians rebuild their country and shape their future in peace and dignity. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Somalia for the brief, for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of France.

Thank you, Madam President. I thank the Deputy Special Envoy, Ambassador Claudia Cordone, and Acting ASG for Humanitarian Affairs, Indrika Wijeratne. and Ms. Rola Roukbi for those briefings which highlighted the progress made by Syria over the past few months, as well as the work that still remains to be done. I also welcome participation from Syria, Qatar, and Turkey in this meeting. Madam President, this month marks the 13th anniversary of the chemical weapons attack perpetrated against the population of the Ghouta and France pays tribute to the victims. Justice must be done and the ending of the chemical weapons regime of the Assad regime participates in this. The historic visit of the President of France to Syria in July illustrates the shared resolve of our two countries, France and Syria, to overcome the legacy of the previous regime, to help Syria turn the page on this tragic chapter of its history and to rebuild anew. This Council ought to send three messages today. First of all, we must continue the efforts underway as part of the political transition to guarantee a just and lasting peace by combating impunity first and foremost. The launch of the trial in absentia of former dictator Bashar al-Assad and members of his regime is an important stage in the process of transitional justice. The work of the national commissions and now of the new Syrian parliament are accelerating with the support of international mechanisms. Next, through consolidating a united and democratic state based upon respect for rule of law and respect for human rights, which brings together all of the elements of the Syrian people and which respects the rights of women who are waiting to take up their rightful place in the Syrian society. France, therefore, welcome the successful integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces within the Syrian state and their dissolution, which is a historic step toward a sovereign and pluralist Syria. After the progress made in the beginning of this year, thanks to recognition of the cultural rights of the Kurds, all Syrian communities, Druze, Alawites, Christians, and others, legitimately expect to be harmoniously integrated into the country's civil space. The parliament will have the great responsibility of leading the country toward elections, and we underscore the importance of the participation of women in Syrian politics. The UN can play a key role in this transition, closer to the ground and respecting the state's sovereignty. Secondly, the recovery and reconstruction of Syria are priorities that the entire international community can contribute to. The removal of Syria from the American list of states sponsored terrorism therefore marks a new step towards the process of lifting sanctions. In parallel, the Syrian authorities are establishing a reliable banking system and a framework to combat corruption to encourage the return of foreign investment. We call on the international community to take part in the reconstruction efforts, including through the restitution of ill-gotten goods. France has led the charge in this regard, after announcing the forthcoming restitution of ill-gotten assets to benefit the Syrian people. This goes hand in hand with continued humanitarian efforts. at a time when almost 15.6 million people are still in urgent need of aid in the country. And we commend the progress made over the past few months with the return of millions of IDPs and refugees. And we are aware that other efforts must be made to ensure their reintegration into the country. Third, the regional integration of Syria is the key to its long-term stability. The Syrian authorities have expressed their will to establish peaceful relations with all of their neighbors and are taking action in this regard. This is worthy of our full support. We encourage the rapprochement with Lebanon, the resumption of security talks between Syria and Israel is a step in the right direction, which we encourage. We call on Israel to stop its destabilizing incursions on Syrian soil and to respect the disengagement of forces agreement of 1974. as well as to fully respect Syrian sovereignty. These actions jeopardize the efforts made by the Syrian government, which are showing maximum restraint. The territorial integrity of Syria is non-negotiable. Lastly, we encourage the Syrian authorities to unwaveringly pursue the fight against terrorism as part of the international coalition against Daesh, which is crucial to the region's security. And as announced by the President of the Republic during his visit to Damascus, the fight against terrorism is a priority for bilateral cooperation between France and Syria. Madam President, Syria has begun a delicate transition, which remains fragile despite the great strides that have been made. To succeed, Syria deserves and needs the support and the trust of our Council. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I thank the representative of France for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Greece.

Thank you, Madam President. And let me thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone and Acting Assistant Secretary General Ratwatte, as well as Ms. Roula Rougby for the valuable contributions. Almost a year since the Security Council's historic visit to Damascus, The Secretary-General's recent visit to Syria marks another important milestone. His presence and engagement there point to a new chapter in Syria's relationship with the UN and most importantly, in the country's future. I wish to underscore three points today. First, progress has been made on both the political transition and transitional justice. Although important challenges remain. Greece continues to support a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political transition, which must be truly inclusive, credible, and sustainable. The protection and meaningful political participations of all Syrians, including women, irrespective of ethnicity or religion, must be guaranteed. This is indispensable for Syria's long-term stability and prosperity. A key institution of the political transition, the composition of the People's Assembly, has been finalized. It must safeguard the meaningful participation of all Syrians, regardless of ethnicity or religion, in the political affairs of their country and start work on a constitution which protects and integrates all components of Syrian society. Its work should also contribute to accountability, the rule of law, and ultimately, a permanent constitutional order enjoying broad legitimacy. We also note progress on transitional justice, which is essential for reconciliation and rebuilding trust amongst the different components of Syrian society. In this context, we also look forward to the adoption of the forthcoming General Assembly resolution on women searches of missing persons, which Greece is proud to co-sponsor. Cooperation with the UN mechanism, including the Triple IM and the Double MP, remains critical in this context. We welcome Syria's renewed cooperation with the OPCW and the restoration of Syria's rights and privileges within the organization clearly demonstrates that constructive engagement with the international community can produce tangible results. The recent breakthrough in cooperation with the IAEA provides another encouraging example of the value of transparency in international engagement. Second, Madam President, we welcome the United States' decision to rescind Syria's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism. This important development can help facilitate reconstruction, investment, and broader economic activity, supporting Syria's recovery and its reconnection with the international community. Prosperity in Syria is key for the prosperity and the stability of the whole region. We are ready to play an active and constructive role to this end. The country's reconstruction can also help create the conditions for the voluntary, safe, and dignified return of Syrians abroad. Third. Turning to the security situation, we are encouraged by signs of de-escalation and by the growing emphasis on dialogue and negotiations following recent concerning developments. We welcome the direct talks between Syria and Israel and sincerely hope that they will yield concrete results. We also acknowledge the constructive role played by the United States and Jordan in this context. Greece reiterates its full respect for Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity. We welcome the implementation of the 29 January agreement to integrate the SDF and all the relevant military-civilian infrastructures in the Syrian State. This was an important step towards an independent and sovereign Syria encompassing all its components. the Sweden Roadmap must be followed up and fully implemented one year after its adoption. In concluding, Madam President, Greece believes that inclusive political transition, justice and accountability, economic recovery and full respect for Syria's sovereignty can together lay the foundations for a peaceful, stable and prosperous future. The odyssey of the Syrian people has been long and arduous. As the end appears to draw near, Greece stands firmly alongside the Syrian people, mindful that the path ahead remains with many challenges. We stand ready to contribute to this endeavor. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Thank you, Madam President. We are grateful for the briefings by Claudio Cordone, the Deputy Special Envoy for Syria, Indrika Ratwatte, the Acting Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs of OCHA, and Rola Rugbi, the country director of Women Now for Development Lebanon. Moreover, we recognize the presence of the representatives of the Syrian Arab Republic, Turkey and Qatar who honor us with their presence. Madam President, Syria is an ancient nation. and it is a fundamental component of human history and civilization. However, for all too long, its people have suffered the consequences of a conflict in which outside interests have turned its territory into the setting of geopolitical rivalries and confrontations. Panama feels that the time has come for Syria to move towards peace and reconstruction. In this regard, we reiterate our commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Syria. Moreover, we believe it is particularly important that legitimate security concerns not be translated into actions or acts of aggression which would further compromise Syrian sovereignty or which would jeopardize the transition that the country is undergoing. In this context, we highlight the efforts, the constructive efforts of the United States to facilitate dialogue mechanisms, and we call upon all parties to prioritize restraint and de-escalation. Despite the enormous challenges which remain, we can see encouraging elements in the Syrian transition process. We believe it is important that the new People's Assembly fully exercise its functions and that it thus contributes to strengthening political representation and the institutional foundations of the transition. Equally, Syria should continue to make progress on transitional justice after more than a decade of conflict. The victims and their families have the right to justice, truth and reparation. We reiterate that the full, meaningful participation of women must continue to occupy a central place in the transition process. it is an essential element for building legitimate and inclusive institutions. This represents an important step towards broader and more effective participation of women in all decision-making spaces. Panama also notes the evolving security situation. We recognize positive progress made by Syria, such as the recently announced process of the peaceful integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces, the SDF, within the Syrian state. We also believe it is important for the international community to continue to support these efforts. Therefore, we believe that the recent decision by the United States to remove Syria from the list of state sponsors of terrorism is timely and appropriate. This measure represents an important show of confidence in the transformation process that the country is undergoing and could help eliminate obstacles which for years have limited Syria's economic and financial reintegration. Economic recovery is another essential element for Syria's stability, not only as a matter of growth, but also as a condition for giving greater opportunities to the population. Madam President, Panama reiterates its firm support for the work of the United Nations in Syria. We would highlight the recent visit by the Secretary-General, and we reiterate our unequivocal support for the relocation of the Office of the Special Envoy to Damascus. We also recognise progress in cooperation between Syrian authorities and UNHCR to facilitate the voluntary, safe and dignified return of refugees. At the same time, the humanitarian situation remains critical. The international community must not reduce the attention it pays to Syria precisely when the country is beginning to enter a new phase of hope. Panama welcomes the recent progress made in Syria's cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency, in particular the decision by the Syrian authorities to declare the presence of nuclear material and to facilitate access for the Agency's inspectors. In broader terms, This progress represents an encouraging sign of Syria's increasing commitment to the multilateral system and to its specialized agencies. Madam President, the path towards a new Syria, one that is rooted in human dignity, the participation of all of its peoples and lasting peace, constitutes an effort that should be highlighted. Panama will continue to support a sovereign, united, stable and peaceful Syria, one that is fully integrated within the international community and that is supported by United Nations that is present and committed to the needs of the Syrian people. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Panama for the statement and I now give the floor to the representative of Bahrain.

Sayed Al Raisi, Madam President. I would like to thank Mr. Claudio Cordoni, Deputy Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria, and Mr. Enrique Ratwate, Assistant Secretary-General for -- Acting Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs. And we took note of Ms. Rola Rugby's briefings. I welcome also the participation of the permanent representatives of the Syrian Republic, the State of Qatar, and the Republic of Turkey. Madam President, the Kingdom of Bahrain follows with interest the political developments in the sisterly Syrian Arab Republic, and we affirm our support for all efforts undertaken by the Syrian Government to strengthen its security and stability, and to preserve Syria's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity and unity. We reject all interference and attacks that would undermine these principles in accordance with the Charter of the UN and international law. The Kingdom believes that Syria is today undergoing a critical phase that requires the international community to unify its efforts in support of the brotherly Syrian people in achieving their legitimate aspirations for security, stability, development and prosperity. In this context, the Kingdom of Bahrain welcomes the announcement by the US to remove the sisterly Syrian Arab Republic from the list of state sponsors of terrorism, considering it a positive step that supports reconstruction effort, economic recovery, and Syria's reintegration into the international community. The Kingdom commends the progress made in building Syrian state institutions, including the convening of the People's Assembly. We appreciate the effort undertaken by the Syrian government and the relevant national committees in the areas of transitional justice and missing persons, which supports national reconciliation and peaceful coexistence and enhances the participation of various components of Syrian society in building the country's future. The Kingdom of Bahrain also welcomes the visit undertaken by His Excellency the Secretary-General to Damascus last July, the first visit by United Nations Secretary-General to Syria since 2009, and the discussions and meetings it included with the Syrian leadership and representatives of the components of the Syrian society.
